newsitem.title: USA: U.S. growth seen below 2 pct in Q2--NY Fed's Peach.
newsitem.headline: U.S. growth seen below 2 pct in Q2--NY Fed's Peach.

text.p: - U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth is likely to slow to below 2.0 percent in the second quarter of 1997, Federal Reserve Bank of New York assistant vice president Richard Peach said on Thursday.

"Recent data suggest growth will slow substantially in the second quarter, likely to under 2.0 percent," Peach, a senior New York Fed economist specialized in the U.S. economy, told the Rockefeller Institute of Government.
"But it is unclear whether this is simply a pause or a transition to slower growth," Peach also said.

Peach noted that, year-over-year, the U.S. GDP rose at a torrid 4.0-percent rate in the first quarter and that economic conditions currently appeared "quite favorable for future growth in the second half" of 1997.
Turning to inflation, Peach noted that "core inflation decelerated further in the first quarter."

"But data for the past three months provide a hint that the rate of increases of prices of core services may be turning upward," Peach said, adding this would be "for the first time in this business cycle."
The current expansion started in April 1991.

Citing data from the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Peach showed that core CPI for goods hovered around 1.0 percent in the past three months, while core CPI for services edged back up after brushing the 3.0-percent level earlier this year.
"We know the economy is going to slow substantially in the second quarter. The question is 'What lies ahead?'," he added.
"Historically, high levels of resource utilization have been associated with accelerating inflation, but with a substantial lag," Peach noted.
The New York Fed senior economist stressed that income growth and a low level of inventories were two factors pointing to good growth in the second half of 1997.

"Real disposable income growth remains quite strong. The savings rate has not plummeted. Spending is being fueled by income growth," Peach added. "The fundamentals of domestic demand remain quite favorable."
Peach pointed out that the expected slower GDP growth in the second quarter is tied to a likely decrease in the rate of build-up in inventories following an unsustainable surge in January-March.
"It's unlikely inventories in the second quarter will contribute as much as they did in the first quarter," Peach said.

However, the New York Fed senior economist also stressed that the recent industrial production data indicate that demand may have depleted inventories and that manufacturers will rebuild them in the second half of 1997, boosting growth.
"Industrial production continued to grow at a rapid rate, giving us the reason to think inventories are relatively lean at this stage," Peach said.
